beats.title: Lesson 4 — Brute-forcing the FUXA HMI
beats.say: Welcome back to CybICS. The H M I is the operator's window onto the process, and their hand on the controls. In this lesson we brute-force the login of the FUXA human-machine interface.

beats.head: A default password on the HMI
beats.body:
FUXA authenticates through a JSON login API with no lockout. Worse, it ships with a default admin password.
  • We target admin and let ffuf try a wordlist, keeping only the successful response.
  • The default, 123456, is the very first guess any list makes.
  • Maps to MITRE ATT&CK for ICS T0812 Default Credentials and T0859 Valid Accounts.
beats.say: FUXA authenticates through a J S O N login A P I, and it has no lockout. Worse, it ships with a default admin password. We target the admin account and let ffuf try a wordlist, keeping only the response that means success. And the default, one two three four five six, is the very first guess any wordlist makes. This maps to default credentials and valid accounts.

beats.caption: Brute-force the FUXA admin login with ffuf
beats.say: We point ffuf at the FUXA sign-in A P I, matching only on a two hundred OK, the sign of a valid login. The very first word is a hit: one two three four five six. The operator interface is protected by the weakest password there is.

beats.head: From HMI login to process control
beats.body: An HMI login is not read-only — it can watch and command the process. To prove the access, we log in over the API, pull the FUXA project, and read the challenge flag from the operator view embedded in it.
beats.say: An H M I login is not a read only status page: it lets you watch the process and send commands to it. To prove the access, we log in over the A P I, pull the FUXA project, and read the challenge flag straight from the operator view embedded inside it.

beats.caption: Log in over the API and read the flag from the HMI project
beats.cmd: TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"username":"admin","password":"123456"}' http://172.18.0.4:1881/api/signin | python3 -c 'import sys,json;print(json.load(sys.stdin)["data"]["token"])'); curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://172.18.0.4:1881/api/project | grep -oiE 'CybICS\([^)<]*\)' | head -1
beats.say: We sign in with the cracked password, take the session token the server hands back, and use it to download the H M I project. Hidden in one of the operator views is the flag: CybICS, F U, hash hash, A. Valid credentials gave us the operator's entire screen.

beats.caption: Submit the flag in the CybICS dashboard - on the attack machine
beats.say: We complete the challenge on the dashboard, opening the FUXA password attack and submitting the flag we lifted from the H M I project.

beats.head: What we learned
beats.body:
• A default password on an HMI hands an attacker operator-level control of the process.
  • The login was a plain API with no lockout — brute force is trivial.
  • Defences: change every default, add lockout and multi-factor, and keep the HMI on an isolated network.
beats.say: To recap: a default password on a human machine interface hands an attacker operator level control of the process, and a plain login A P I with no lockout makes brute force trivial. The defences are the familiar ones: change every default credential, add lockout and multi factor authentication, and keep the H M I on an isolated network.

beats.title: Flag captured: CybICS(FU##A)
beats.sub: Next lesson: brute-forcing the OpenPLC login  ·  github.com/mniedermaier/CybICS
beats.say: Flag captured. In the next lesson we do the same to the OpenP L C controller's own web login.
